Topic 01

PCOS & movement

With PCOS, more intensity is not always better. The right mix of strength work, low-impact cardio and recovery can support insulin sensitivity and energy without spiking stress hormones. Here's what I've seen actually work.

Resistance training is the single most useful tool for most of my PCOS clients - it supports insulin sensitivity and body composition without the cortisol load of daily high-intensity sessions. Keep it simple: squat, hinge, push, pull, carry.

A daily 30-minute walk does more for blood sugar and stress than flogging yourself with HIIT five days a week. If you love high-intensity work, keep it to once or twice a week and watch how your body responds.

With PCOS, progress often shows up as better sleep, steadier energy and more regular cycles before it shows up as weight change. Those wins count - write them down.

Topic 02

Endometriosis & exercise

Endo isn't a reason to stop moving - but it is a reason to move differently. The goal is a body that feels safer and stronger, on your good days and your rough ones.

Flare days call for breathwork, gentle mobility and heat, not heroics. Better days can hold strength and Pilates. A flexible weekly plan beats a rigid one you abandon every month.

Low-load core and pelvic-floor-aware Pilates builds support around the pelvis without bracing or gripping. In my studio it's the modality endo clients stick with longest.

Chronic pain keeps the system on high alert. Slow breathing, long exhales and restorative positions aren't "skipping" a session - they're part of the program.

Topic 03

Weight loss that sticks

After a decade in this work, here's the honest version: the plan that works is the one you can live with. Sustainable beats perfect, every single time.

Three sessions a week you actually do beats six you abandon by week three. Start smaller than your motivation wants to - consistency compounds.

Strength training protects your metabolism while you lose weight and changes how your body looks and feels long before the scale catches up. Keep protein and lifting in the picture.

One big weekend doesn't undo a good month, and one salad doesn't make one. Zoom out to the weekly average and the pressure drops - and so does the rebound eating.

Topic 04

Getting (back) into activity

Whether you're starting from zero or coming back after kids, injury or a long break - the first eight weeks matter more than any program detail.

Ten minutes counts. A walk around the block counts. The habit of showing up is worth more than the content of the session for the first month.

After the school drop-off, before your shower, during your lunch break. Anchoring a new habit to an old one is the most reliable behaviour-change trick I know.

Pilates, swimming, dancing in the kitchen, bushwalking - the best exercise is the one you'll still be doing in winter. Give yourself permission to experiment.

Topic 05

Falls, balance & staying steady

Falls are common after 65, but they are not inevitable - balance is a skill, and skills can be trained at any age. This is some of the most rewarding work I do with older clients.

Standing balance work - heel-to-toe walking, single-leg stands with a fingertip of support - practiced little and often is what teaches your body to catch itself. It starts wobbly for everyone. That is the point.

Sit-to-stands from a chair, heel raises at the bench, step-ups on the bottom stair. Leg strength is what turns a trip into a wobble instead of a fall.

Vision, medications, foot health, loose rugs and dim hallways all play a part. A yearly medication review with the GP and an eye check belong in every falls plan - alongside the training, not instead of it.

Topic 06

Fibroids & movement

Fibroids are common, and most people with them can keep moving well. The trick is working with your symptoms - heavy days, pelvic pressure, fatigue - instead of pretending they're not there.

On heavy or crampy days, swap impact for breathwork, gentle mobility and restorative Pilates. On good days, train normally. A flexible week beats a rigid program you keep abandoning.

Resistance training is usually well tolerated with fibroids, and it supports body composition and bone health. Build gradually - and if heavy bracing ramps up pelvic pressure, swap to lighter loads and higher reps.

Heavy bleeding can drain iron stores, which shows up as breathlessness and exhaustion in sessions. If that sounds like you, it's worth a blood test and a chat with your GP - and shorter sessions in the meantime.

Topic 07

Arthritis & movement

Arthritis is not a reason to stop moving - most joints do better with regular, well-dosed movement than with rest alone. The art is finding the dose that helps without stirring things up.

Gentle range-of-motion work most days keeps stiff joints gliding more freely. Slow, comfortable circles and swings - a few minutes morning and evening beats one heroic session a week.

Strength around the joint - hips, knees, shoulders, hands - shares the load the joint has to carry. Start low, progress slowly, and keep a lighter version of every session for rough days.

Some ache with new exercise is normal; pain that flares and lingers into the next day is the sign to dial back. Adjust the dose - don't abandon the movement.

Topic 08

Type 2 diabetes & exercise

Movement is one of the most powerful everyday tools for steadier blood sugar - and it doesn't take punishing workouts. With type 2 diabetes, consistency quietly beats intensity.

A 10 to 15 minute walk after eating helps working muscles soak up glucose while levels are on the rise. It's the simplest habit I give clients with T2D, and the one that tends to stick.

Strength training two or three times a week builds the tissue that uses the most glucose, supporting insulin sensitivity over time. Simple moves, moderate loads, done regularly.

If you use insulin or certain medications, exercise can shift blood sugar more than expected. Work out your own patterns with your GP or diabetes educator, and keep a quick carb snack handy just in case.

Topic 09

Fatty liver & lifestyle

Fatty liver responds to lifestyle change better than almost any condition I see - regular movement genuinely moves the needle, even before the scale shifts much.

Brisk walking, cycling, swimming - regular moderate aerobic work is the best-studied movement for reducing liver fat. Most days of the week, built up gradually, is the goal.

Two to three resistance sessions a week support insulin sensitivity and body composition, which both matter for liver health. Keep it simple and repeatable.

Even modest weight loss - around 5 percent of body weight - can meaningfully reduce liver fat for many people. Slow and sustainable beats dramatic and short-lived, here as everywhere.

Pilates, from mat to reformer

Nine years of teaching - mat, reformer, and pre & post natal. Here's what each one actually looks like.

The studio

How we move together

Pilates is the heart of my work. Whether you're on the mat at home, on the reformer in the studio, or moving through pregnancy and new parenthood - the goal is the same: deep strength, easier movement, and a body you trust.

Mat work uses your own body weight plus small props - the ring, the ball, the band - to build deep core control and mobility. It's the foundation everything else stands on, and it travels anywhere: studio, lounge room, hotel floor.

The reformer's springs can support you or challenge you, which makes it endlessly adjustable: precise, low-impact strength for beginners, injury recovery and older clients - and a serious workout for the strong. It's where I spend most of my teaching hours.

Pregnancy-safe modifications trimester by trimester, then a patient postpartum rebuild of core and pelvic floor - at your pace, with your healthcare provider's clearance. Strong and calm beats fast and sore, every time.

Hi, I'm Sherri.

I'm an Accredited Exercise Physiologist with 11 years of experience, and I've spent 9 of those teaching Pilates - mat, reformer, and pre & post natal. Over the years I've worked with elderly clients and with people of all ages living with metabolic and neurological conditions, helping each person feel at home in their body again.

I started Gold Rehab because the best advice I've ever given wasn't complicated - it was honest, practical and kind. This site is where I share the things that actually work: for PCOS, endometriosis, weight loss, and for anyone who just wants to feel strong and capable again.

No shame, no 30-day shreds, no before-and-after pressure. Just real guidance from real experience.
